plain_title: Recording a suicide attempt so care stays focused on safety
one_liner: A proposed category for people who've made a suicide attempt within the past two years, to keep safety central.
in_simple_words: Suicidal behavior disorder is a proposed, not official, category for someone who has made a suicide attempt in the past two years. It isn't a disorder of character; it records that an attempt happened so that care keeps safety and follow-up at the centre, whatever other diagnosis a person has. A past attempt is the strongest single predictor of future risk, and most people who survive an attempt do not die by suicide. Follow-up matters most in the months afterwards.
what_it_can_feel_like: After my attempt I was discharged with a leaflet. Six months later a different hospital gave me a safety plan, a follow-up call every week, and a therapist. That's the version that worked.
Nobody tells you the first year after is the hardest and the most important. Weekly calls got me through it.
common_signs: A suicide attempt within the last two years
Recorded regardless of any other diagnosis
Not applied to self-injury without intent to die
Signals the need for safety planning and follow-up

myths_vs_facts.myth: Once someone has attempted, they'll always be at risk.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Risk is highest in the months after and falls with time and support. Most attempt survivors go on to live, and many describe deep relief that they did.

how_common.plain: Attempts are far more common than deaths; estimates suggest many attempts for every death. Most people who attempt survive and recover.
how_common.figure: WHO estimates attempts outnumber deaths many times over; over 720,000 suicide deaths worldwide each year (2025 fact sheet)
how_common.note: Present carefully; avoid numbers that sensationalise.

what_helps.plain_summary: What helps after an attempt: a safety plan made with a clinician, rapid follow-up (a call or visit within days, not weeks), therapy that targets suicidal thinking (CBT for suicide prevention, DBT, CAMS), treatment of any underlying condition with any medication prescribed and monitored by a doctor, involving trusted people, and making the environment safer. Brief contact interventions, like follow-up messages, reduce repeat attempts. Peer support with other attempt survivors helps with shame and isolation.
evidence_based_options: Safety planning and rapid follow-up after discharge
CBT for suicide prevention, DBT, or CAMS
Treatment of underlying depression, trauma, substance use, or other conditions
Brief contact follow-up and peer support for attempt survivors
self_help_that_supports_care: Keeping your safety plan where you can find it
Telling one person you trust what helps when things get dark
Attending follow-up even when you feel better
Peer groups where attempt survivors talk openly

when_to_reach_out: If you've attempted and are struggling again, reach out now: a crisis line from the strip, a trusted person, or an emergency department. If you're supporting someone after an attempt, ask directly how they are, help them keep follow-up appointments, and keep the lines of contact open.
is_not: Nonsuicidal self-injury, done to cope rather than to die, is recorded separately. Suicidal thoughts without an attempt are covered on the suicidal thoughts card.
hope_note: Most attempt survivors are alive years later, and many become the people who help others through. The period after an attempt is when support changes everything.

content_notes: Safe-messaging rules apply: no methods, no numbers.
